newsitem.title: CUBA: Britain will help Cuba fight drug trafficking.
newsitem.headline: Britain will help Cuba fight drug trafficking.

text.p: Britain and Cuba signed an accord on Wednesday on combating drug trafficking, saying cooperation was needed as the Caribbean island became increasingly important as a transit point for smugglers.

Thomas Sackville, the visiting deputy minister of Britain's Home Office, signed the agreement with Cuban customs chief Gen. Pedro Pupo. Sackville also donated eight motorscooters to the anti-drugs department of the police.

"We know that there is the potential in this country for the (drug-trafficking) situation to become very bad ... but we know that there is a chance to arrest the problem now," Sackville told reporters after the ceremony at the Foreign Ministry.
"The commitment of Cuba in the fight against drugs is absolute," Sackville said. "The use of information we have provided Cuba has been exemplary and has led to some very significant arrests."

Sackville said the agreement, which includes provisions for the exchange of information and the training of Cuban drug officers by British experts, aimed at cementing existing cooperation on the drug problem.

British officials said information provided by Britain in recent months had helped Cuba intercept mules -- people used by drug rings to transport drugs on commercial flights -- and vessels carrying drugs.
British information contributed to the seizure of about 440 pounds (200 kg) of drugs this year, the officials said.

Cuban officials noted they had seen a huge rise in drug seizures this year, partly because of the island's growing importance as a transit point for drugs going from Latin America to North America or Europe and partly because of more effective police and customs work.

Oliveiro Montalvo, head of the Cuban police's anti-drug department, said 2.75 tons (2.5 tonnes) of drugs had been seized so far in 1996, mostly cocaine and marijuana but also some heroin. This compared with just 22 pounds (10 kg) of drugs seized in all of 1995, he added.
Seventy-three people, 63 of them foreigners, have been arrested on suspicion of involvement in drug trafficking, compared with just six foreigners arrested in 1995.
Cuban state media have given a high profile to many of the police operations this year and stressed that traffickers arrested in Cuba would face stiff penalties.

Montalvo, who said drug consumption in Cuba itself was still not a significant problem, said Cuba was eager to cooperate with other countries in combating drug smuggling. He reiterated Cuba's view that cooperation could extend to the United States if Washington wanted.

Cuba, long at odds with the United States, has angrily rejected allegations leveled in the U.S. that it is not doing enough to halt drug smuggling and that there may be Cuban involvement in some trafficking.
